transcript.content: Hello, welcome. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you. Um, well, it's a little complicated, I guess, or maybe it's not, but what finally pushed me to actually make this appointment and come in today is... well, it's this issue I'm having with just staying in my chair. 

I'm a software developer, and we have these sprint planning meetings—which, if you know anything about software, you know they can be incredibly long and tedious, but they're really important for figuring out our workflow for the next couple of weeks. And I know I should stay put. I know I need to be sitting there, looking at the screen, participating. But I just keep getting up. Like, right in the middle of someone talking, I'll suddenly decide I absolutely need a glass of water right that very second, or I'll just get up to check something in the other room that completely doesn't matter and could definitely wait. 

And it's not even just at work, which is the frustrating part! I do it during personal stuff, too. We've been on these really important mortgage calls lately, which are dry, sure, but obviously I need to be present for them. And I'll do the exact same thing—I'll just stand up and walk away from the laptop to go wander into the kitchen, even though I know I'm supposed to be sitting there listening to the broker. I just... I can't seem to just stay seated when I know I'm supposed to, and it's starting to really make me feel like I'm losing my grip on my own actions.
Looking back at your childhood, particularly before the age of 12, did you experience similar difficulties with sitting still or restlessness?

Oh, wow, yes. Absolutely. In fact, when you ask that, it immediately makes me think of... gosh, it must have been third grade? Or maybe fourth? I had this teacher, Mrs. Gable, and I remember she actually had to move my desk. Like, she completely separated me from the little groups or pods we were supposed to sit in. Because I was just constantly popping up out of my chair. 

It wasn't even that I was trying to be bad or rebellious, I just... I would think of something, or I'd drop a pencil, or I'd see something happening at the pencil sharpener, and before I even realized I was making a decision to move, I was already standing up. She was always, *always* having to stop the lesson to remind me to sit back down. 

And it wasn't just the standing up, honestly. It was the talking, too. I remember getting so frustrated because I knew the answers, right? Like, I understood the material perfectly fine, but I just could not wait for her to actually call my name. I would just blurt things out right over other kids. And because I understood the work, I would just absolutely rush through all my assignments. I'd fly through my math worksheets in like five minutes just to get them done, and then I'd be sitting there bored, which probably made the standing up and wandering around even worse, now that I think about it. 

My parents used to get these notes sent home, or at parent-teacher conferences it was always the exact same story—"She's a bright girl, she gets the concepts, but she just rushes through everything, talks out of turn, and will not stay in her seat." It's actually kind of ironic, I guess, that I'm 40 years old and I'm basically doing the exact same thing in my corporate meetings now that I was doing in Mrs. Gable's classroom. I just... I really thought I would have outgrown that by now, you know? But it's like the minute I feel that urge to move or speak, the logic part of my brain just totally lags behind what my body is already doing.
Aside from feeling the urge to get up and move, do you have trouble sustaining your attention on tasks or projects until they are finished?

Oh, definitely. It's actually really frustrating because I always go in with the best intentions, you know? Like, take my work for example. As a developer, a big part of my job is reviewing other people's code—we call them pull requests. And I'll sit down, open the pull request on my monitor, and tell myself, 'Okay, I am going to read through this logic, I'm going to find any bugs, I'm going to be super thorough.' 

And for the first minute or two, I'm right there. But then... I don't even know how it happens, honestly. I'll just suddenly realize that I've been staring at the exact same block of code for I don't know how long, and I haven't actually processed a single line of it. Because my brain is suddenly thinking about five completely unrelated things all at once. Like, did I leave the coffee maker on? What am I going to make for dinner? I need to text my sister back about her birthday plans, oh, and I wonder if that package I ordered shipped yet. 

And it happens with the personal stuff too, like those mortgage documents I mentioned earlier! My husband and I were trying to read through the disclosures last night, and they are so incredibly dense, but I really, truly wanted to understand them because it's a huge financial commitment, obviously. But the exact same thing happened. I can start reading the documents with totally good intentions, but after a few minutes, I realize I'm just staring at the exact same section on the page, completely zoned out, thinking about my grocery list or an email I forgot to send. It just feels like I can't keep my brain tethered to the thing I'm actually supposed to be looking at, no matter how hard I try to force it, which just makes every single project take so much longer than it actually should.
